items.title: [Sports Science 101 #12] One Body, Many Ages: Why Exercise Should Change As You Grow
items.body:
> The way your body responds to exercise shifts from childhood to old age, and matching your training to your life stage is what keeps you strong, mobile, and healthy for decades.

## Today's Concept

There is no single "correct" workout that fits a person for their whole life. The same body needs different things at age 8, 18, 45, and 75, because it is doing different jobs at each stage: building, peaking, maintaining, and preserving.

A few ideas explain most of it:

- **Kids are still building the frame.** The long bones of children and teens grow at soft zones called **growth plates**, near the ends of the bones. Because kids are constructing coordination and bone at the same time, the priority is *variety and skill*, not heavy loads. The old fear that lifting weights "stunts" a child's growth is not supported by the research. Under good coaching, resistance training is safe and helpful for youth. The real danger is bad technique or trying to lift maximal weight without supervision.

- **Teens hit a growth spurt, then a strength spurt.** During puberty there is a stretch of fastest growth called **Peak Height Velocity (PHV)** — roughly ages 11–12 in girls and 13–14 in boys. Limbs grow before coordination catches up, which is why teens can suddenly look clumsy. Big gains in muscle and strength tend to arrive *after* that height spurt, especially once hormones ramp up.

- **Adults are managing a peak.** Bone mineral density tops out in the late 20s to early 30s. After about age 30, adults slowly lose muscle if they do nothing — a process called **sarcopenia**. Exercise here is maintenance: keep the aerobic engine and the muscle you already built.

- **Older adults are preserving independence.** After 60, muscle and bone loss speed up, and falls become a serious risk. Strength and balance training is not about looking athletic; it is about carrying groceries, climbing stairs, and getting up off the floor safely.

The headline: youth *builds the bank*, adulthood *protects the balance*, and later life *spends it slowly*.

## In Everyday Life

Picture the Martinez family in Ohio, all under one roof.

Eight-year-old Mateo plays in a Little League that costs about $120 for the season. His parents wonder if they should get him "serious" with a weight program. The better bet is what he is already doing — running, throwing, climbing, switching sports across the year. That variety builds coordination and banks bone density he will keep for life.

His sister Sofia, 14, just shot up four inches and keeps tripping over her own feet in soccer. That is PHV at work, not a lack of talent. Her strength gains are coming — they usually follow the height spurt.

Their mom, 46, pays $60 a month for a gym membership but mostly does the treadmill. Adding two short strength sessions a week is what actually fights the muscle loss that has quietly started. And Grandpa, 74, doesn't need a bodybuilder's routine — a few sit-to-stand reps from a kitchen chair and some balance work meaningfully lower his odds of a fall, one of the most common reasons older Americans lose their independence.

Same house, four bodies, four different exercise "prescriptions."

## 3-Line Summary

1. Exercise is not one-size-fits-all; the goal changes with age — build, peak, maintain, then preserve.
2. Supervised resistance training does not stunt kids' growth; the growth-spurt clumsiness of teens is normal and temporary.
3. Bone and muscle you build young are a "bank" you draw on later, so strength and balance training matters most in older age.

## ✅ Self Quiz

1. **True or False:** Properly supervised resistance training stunts a child's growth by damaging the growth plates.
2. **Peak Height Velocity (PHV)** refers to:
   - A) The maximum sprint speed a teen can reach
   - B) The period of fastest height growth during puberty
   - C) The age when bone density peaks
3. **True or False:** The main reason to prioritize strength and balance training for adults over 65 is to reduce the risk of falls and preserve independence.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Growth plate (epiphyseal plate):** A zone of cartilage near the ends of a child's long bones where lengthening happens; it hardens and closes after puberty.
- **Peak Height Velocity (PHV):** The point during puberty when a person grows in height fastest, typically earlier in girls than boys.
- **Sarcopenia:** The age-related loss of muscle mass and strength that begins around age 30 and speeds up in later decades.
- **Bone mineral density:** A measure of how much mineral is packed into bone; it peaks in the late 20s to early 30s and is built partly through weight-bearing activity when young.
- **Physical literacy:** The foundation of movement skills — running, jumping, throwing, balancing — that a child develops through varied, playful activity.

---
*Answers: 1) False — under proper supervision, resistance training is considered safe for youth and does not stunt growth; injuries come from poor technique or unsupervised maximal lifting, not from strength training itself. 2) B — PHV is the phase of fastest height growth in puberty, roughly ages 11–12 in girls and 13–14 in boys, and it often arrives before coordination and strength catch up. 3) True — for older adults, strength and balance work mainly protects against falls and helps preserve everyday independence.*
